At the edge of the map, where the ink thins into blue, there was a little town that kept a lighthouse even though no sea had ever reached it.

Every evening, the keeper climbed the spiral stairs and lit the lamp. Its beam swept over rooftops, gardens, and the dark fields beyond. The townspeople said it was foolish. Ships did not sail through wheat.

Then, one winter night, a boy arrived carrying a wet oar.

He had crossed a sea that wasn’t there, he said—a sea of fog, with no stars above it and no shore anywhere. He had followed the lighthouse until his boat scraped the stones.

After that, nobody called the lighthouse foolish. The keeper kept the lamp burning, and the townspeople began leaving small offerings by the door: a cup of tea, a dry scarf, a loaf of bread.

Years later, when the boy had grown old, he climbed the stairs himself. From the top, he watched the beam move slowly across the fields.

Somewhere out there, he knew, someone was lost.

Somewhere out there, the dark was only waiting for a light.
